title: The flat line on the capnograph
objective: Monitor a patient during and after moderate sedation within the nurse's scope
secondaryObjectives: Apply pre- and post-procedure standards: consent, timeout and monitoring

brief.situation: 14:00 on a medical-surgical unit. Dr. Lee, the surgeon, is debriding a leg wound at the bedside of Mr. Brandt, 63, under moderate sedation. You are the nurse assigned only to monitor him and give the ordered sedation. He has obstructive sleep apnea.
handover: Consent signed; time-out done. The provider has ordered the sedative and the opioid in small increments by the nurse, titrated to moderate sedation, with the reversal agents at the bedside.

Unit sedation policy: capnography and pulse oximetry continuously, blood pressure every 5 minutes, supplemental oxygen, and stop further doses, support the airway and call rapid response for loss of the capnography waveform, a respiratory rate under 8 or a patient who rouses only to pain.
The rapid response team is two minutes away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and act as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: The capnograph has gone flat and Mr. Brandt won't answer. What is happening, and what do you do?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: A flat capnograph with pauses, slow breathing and response only to pain is deep sedation with hypoventilation; capnography shows it before the saturation falls; sleep apnea raises the risk.
parts.modelAnswer: He's gone past moderate into deep sedation and is hypoventilating: the capnograph is flat during pauses and he responds only to pain. His sleep apnea makes this likelier, and capnography shows it before the saturation drops.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: No more doses; surgeon pauses; jaw thrust and bag-mask ready; oxygen; rapid response; the ordered reversal agent by order; hand off.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the doses, ask the surgeon to pause, open his airway with a jaw thrust, bag-mask ready, call rapid response and get the ordered reversal agent.

noProgress.rationale: A deeply sedated patient still unrescued an hour on is harm here.

expertPath.text: Capnography, oximetry and oxygen on; airway equipment ready.
Sedation level: rousable to voice. Reassess.
Stop doses; pause; rapid response; reversal ready; hand off.

unsafe.headline: Another increment
unsafe.body: Grimacing is not a reason to deepen sedation in a patient already slipping. Reassess before every increment.

worsened.headline: Hypoxic arrest
worsened.body: Capnography warns minutes before the saturation falls. Act on a flat waveform at once.

wrongRoute.headline: Let the procedure finish
wrongRoute.body: The monitoring nurse can stop the procedure. A patient past moderate sedation is rescued first.

target.headline: Rescued in time
target.body: Monitoring before the first dose, the sedation level checked, and the change acted on within minutes. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: Rescued, with delays
recovered.body: Check how soon monitoring started and how long the flat waveform went before you acted.

scoring.modelReasoning: Moderate sedation means a designated nurse monitors with capnography, pulse oximetry and oxygen from before the first increment, with blood pressure every 5 minutes and reversal agents at hand. Sleep apnea raises the risk. A flat capnograph with pauses and response only to pain is deep sedation with hypoventilation: no more doses, the surgeon pauses, the airway is supported, rapid response comes and the ordered reversal agent is given by order.

capQ.explain: Continually monitor ventilatory function with capnography; pulse oximetry falls later, especially on supplemental oxygen.
